newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers vote to lift roadblocks.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers vote to lift roadblocks.

text.p: The main farmers' committee voted on Sunday to lift a 24-day road blockade which has cut Greece in two, caused transport chaos and cost the economy more than $100 million, committee members said.
The Thessaly farmers' committee, where the revolt began in November, called for all barricades to be lifted after a stormy marathon meeting, they told reporters.
An official announcement of the decision, along with details of whether it was a permanent move or just a suspension for the Christmas holidays, was expected during the day, they said.
Farmers from the northern Macedonia and Thrace farm regions lifted their blockades on Saturday and said they would meet socialist Prime Minister Costas Simitis on Monday.

Reporters at the scene in Thessaly, the last bastion of defiance, said smaller roadblocks had come down in the farm heartland in central Greece, stretching from Larissa to Volos on the mainland's eastern coast.
But four massive barricades, composed of thousands of farm tractors, remained around Larissa itself and traffic was still being stopped after the Thessaly committee's decision.

Committee members said the main question was whether the militant farmers around Larissa would abide by the decision to lift the barricades and let thousands of Greeks drive home from the cities to their villages for Christmas holidays.
About five major blockades at Volos, halfway between Athens and Greece's second city of Salonika in the north, were still in place but farmers said they would come down during the day.
The farmers have been demanding lower fuel prices, higher price supports and the rescheduling of $1.3 billion in debts.

Simitis has ruled out any concessions, saying there is no more money to give. He has refused to meet the farmers directly to discuss their problems until they lift their blockades but has also refused to use force to remove them from the roads.

The result has been transport chaos, with hundreds of lorries trapped at blockades, overland transport at a standstill and business leaders enraged over heavy losses -- now estimated at far in excess of $100 million.
If Larissa farmers go along with their committee's decision and lift the blockades, would be the latest in a string of successes for Simitis this weekend.

His 1997 budget, which sparked a range of strikes and protests, easily passed parliament in the early hours of Sunday and a seamen's strike which had crippled ports for five days was called off late on Friday.
Simitis has dished out tough talk to the public, saying his unpopular measures were the only way to ensure the economy would be ready to join a planned single European currency by 2001.
He told parliament before the midnight vote on the budget that he "would not bend" and all Greeks would have to make sacrifices to help achieve convergence with other European Union economies.
The alternative, he said, was isolation which would be "a national disaster" and "lead to the Albanisation of the Greek economy".
